extracted.intended_audience: corporate IP managers, in-house counsel, inventors, startup founders, and IP professionals
extracted.subtask_description: A four-factor decision framework to help companies choose whether to protect an innovation by patenting it or keeping it as a trade secret (or both), taking into account business goals, competitive landscape, enforceability, and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business goals and competitive landscape (threshold inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: A threshold inquiry involves careful analysis of the company’s business goals and its competitive landscape, including identifying competitors, evaluating their IP strategies, the strength of their IP portfolios, and their litigation profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this analysis to gauge how crowded the space is and to refine IP strategy. Example guidance from the page: if competitors have strong or growing patent portfolios, file patents more aggressively to block encroachment and deter lawsuits; if patents are not aggressively sought in the industry, consider relying more on trade secrets. This is an overarching filter applied before the four-factor scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental attributes of patents vs. trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents grant exclusionary rights (making/using/selling) for roughly 20 years and require rigorous examination for novelty and non-obviousness; they are relatively expensive and take time to obtain. Trade secrets protect confidential information indefinitely so long as secrecy is maintained, but they are only enforceable against misappropriation and not when the information is reverse engineered or independently developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade secret protection requires reasonable measures to maintain secrecy (e.g., marking confidential, restricting/logging access, passwords). The company’s mere intent to keep information secret is insufficient. Consider time-to-grant, cost, geographical scope, and enforcement burdens when comparing these fundamental attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the invention is critical—that is, whether it provides the company a competitive edge (e.g., increases adoption, safety, performance, or durability). Patents are useful to the extent they can prevent competitors from offering valuable features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an invention is critical and cannot be practically or reasonably designed around, patent protection is likely to deliver more value. If practical design-arounds exist, the value of patent protection is reduced. Use criticality scoring to favor patents when the invention meaningfully blocks competitor offerings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to reverse engineer
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how easily the innovation can be reverse engineered or independently developed. Trade secret protection is not useful for innovations that can be easily reverse engineered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the technology type (e.g., formulas/compositions are often hard to reverse engineer; hardware and software may be easier to reverse engineer via teardown or black-box testing). The easier it is to reverse engineer, the more the balance shifts toward patent protection; conversely, the harder it is to reverse engineer, the more valuable trade secret protection becomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detectability
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how detectable the claimed invention is in a competitor’s product or process. To enforce a patent, the patentee must show a competitor infringes every element of at least one claim; hard-to-detect elements make enforcement more difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventions tied to front-end, customer-visible features that are easily detectable are good candidates for patents. Back-end functionality or internal processes that are not accessible to end users require analysis of whether the element can be detected through reasonable efforts and whether secrecy can be maintained. Up-front claim-scope analysis and drafting to maximize enforceability is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty in keeping secret (practicality and cost of secrecy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how feasible it is to maintain the invention as a trade secret by considering the nature of the information, the measures required to keep it secret, the number of employees needing access, and the sophistication and flight risk of those employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate costs and practicalities: establish processes for confidentiality, train employees on duties to maintain secrecy, monitor access and departures, and implement logging and access controls. If maintaining secrecy is impractical or cost-prohibitive given business operations and personnel, favor patent protection (or a hybrid approach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring framework, customization, and hybrid strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a multi-factor scoring table (the article’s table assigns higher scores toward patents and lower scores toward trade secrets) to decide which form of protection suits an innovation; the decision is not always mutually exclusive—patents and trade secrets can be used together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should customize possible scores for each factor and the cutoff between patent vs. trade secret to align with overall goals and resource allocation, and reevaluate scoring over time. Example hybrid: patent a manufacturing process while keeping a specific material/component or process parameter as a trade secret. Also consider enforceability, relative costs, and industry norms when setting cutoffs.
